games.name: Battleship
games.blurb: Hunt the hidden fleet cell by cell: every hit is a clue, every miss a wasted shell.
games.howto: Each player has hidden ships on a grid. Take turns firing at squares: X means a hit, a dot means water. Sink the whole enemy fleet first to win.
games.rules:
BATTLESHIP - 6x6 grid, 3 ships each.

GOAL
Each player has a hidden fleet on their own 6x6 grid. Sink all of your opponent's ships before
they sink yours.

SETUP (done by the arena, randomly)
Fleet of each player: Cruiser (3 cells, letter C), Destroyer (2 cells, letter D), Patrol boat (2 cells, letter P) = 7 ship cells.
Ships are straight lines (horizontal or vertical), never overlap, may touch each other, and stay
inside the grid. You see your own ships; you never see the opponent's ships.

COORDINATES
Columns are letters a..f from left to right, rows are numbers 1..6 from top to bottom.
A cell is column letter + row number: "a1" is the top-left corner, "f6" the bottom-right.

TURN ORDER
Player 0 shoots first, then Player 1, alternating. One "round" = Player 0's turn + Player 1's turn.
Each turn you fire exactly ONE shot.

ACTION FORMAT
    fire <cell>
where <cell> is a cell you have never fired at before.
Examples:  "fire c4"   "fire a1"   "fire f6"
Firing at a cell you already fired at, a cell outside the grid, or any other text is illegal
(first time: a warning and the same turn again; second time: you lose the game). Case and extra
spaces do not matter.

FEEDBACK
After each shot you learn: "miss" (water), "hit" (a ship was hit; the ship is not named), or
"hit, sunk <Ship name> (<size>)" when that shot hit the last remaining cell of a ship.
You also see where the opponent's shots landed on your own grid.

WHAT YOU OBSERVE
- Status of both fleets (which ships are sunk), round number, how many shots you must fire.
- YOUR SHOTS grid (the opponent's waters):  . = not fired yet, o = miss, X = hit, # = hit on a ship
  that is already sunk.
- YOUR WATERS grid (your fleet): a ship letter = intact part of your ship, * = part of your ship
  that was hit, o = opponent's miss, . = untouched water.
- The recent shot history of both players.
Example (top-left of a YOUR SHOTS grid):
    a b c d
 1  . o . .
 2  . X X .
 3  # # o .
Meaning: misses at b1 and c3, hits at b2 and c2 (that ship is not sunk yet), and a sunk 2-cell
ship at a3-b3.

HOW THE GAME ENDS AND IS SCORED
The game is checked at the END of every round, so both players always get the same number of turns:
- if only one player has sunk the whole enemy fleet, that player wins;
- if both did it in the same round (Player 1 equalised on the last turn), it is a draw.
Shot cap: after round 30 the game ends; the player who hit more enemy ship cells wins,
equal = draw. Score = number of enemy ship cells you hit (max 7).

fire <cell>
where <cell> is a cell you have never fired at before.
Examples:  "fire c4"   "fire a1"   "fire f6"
Firing at a cell you already fired at, a cell outside the grid, or any other text is illegal
(first time: a warning and the same turn again; second time: you lose the game). Case and extra
spaces do not matter.

games.name: Bulls and Cows
games.blurb: A code-breaking race: both crack each other's secret code at once, and every clue counts.
games.howto: Each player tries to crack the other's secret code. Every guess reveals how many symbols are right and in place, and how many are right but misplaced. First to crack it wins.
games.rules:
BULLS AND COWS - 4 digits, no repeats. 2 players, a simultaneous code-breaking race.

SECRET CODES
The arena gives each player a secret code of 4 digits from 0-9. All 4 digits are DIFFERENT (no repeats), and your guesses must also use 4 different digits.
Your opponent tries to crack YOUR code and you try to crack THEIRS. You see your own code
(it does not affect your play) but never the opponent's.

EACH ROUND
Both players submit one guess at the opponent's code at the same time. Each guess gets
feedback:
  - BULLS: how many positions hold exactly the right symbol;
  - COWS: how many further symbols are in the code but at a different position.
Counting with repeats works like Mastermind: for every symbol, take the smaller of its count
in the guess and in the code, add these up, and subtract the bulls; the rest are cows.
Example: code 4721, guess 1724 -> 2 bulls, 2 cows.

END AND SCORING
- Crack the code (a guess with 4 bulls) to win. If both players crack in the same round, the
  game is a draw.
- Move cap: at most 10 rounds. If nobody has cracked by then, the player whose BEST guess
  had more bulls wins; equal bulls -> more cows in that best guess wins; still equal -> draw.
Your score = bulls of your best guess.

ACTION FORMAT
    guess <code>      exactly 4 digits from 0-9, all different
The word "guess" is optional. Examples: "guess 0123", "guess 9876", "guess 4721".
A guess with the wrong length, other symbols, or repeated symbols is illegal
(first time: a warning and the same turn again; second time: you lose the game).
The legal-actions list is null (too many possible codes).

WHAT YOU OBSERVE EACH TURN
The round number, your own secret code, all your previous guesses with their feedback, and all
your opponent's previous guesses at your code with their feedback.

games.name: Colonel Blotto
games.blurb: Split your army across battlefields in secret: outguess where your rival goes heavy and where they gamble.
games.howto: Each round both players secretly split their soldiers across several battlefields. The bigger army takes each battlefield; take the most valuable share to win the round, and win the most rounds.
games.rules:
COLONEL BLOTTO - 100 soldiers, 5 equal fields. 2 players, simultaneous moves, 5 rounds.

GOAL
Win more rounds than your opponent.

EACH ROUND
There are 5 battlefields, called F1 F2 F3 F4 F5 (in this order, left to right).
All battlefields are worth the same (1 point each).
Every round each player has exactly 100 soldiers to place (a fresh army each round).
Both players secretly choose how many soldiers to put on each battlefield, at the same time.
Then both allocations are revealed. On each battlefield the player with MORE soldiers captures
it; equal soldiers (including 0 vs 0) = nobody captures it.
A round is won by the player who captures MORE battlefields. Equal numbers = the
round is drawn (nobody wins it).

END AND SCORING
After 5 rounds, the player who won more rounds wins the game. If rounds won are equal, the
player who captured more battlefield points over the whole game wins; if that is equal too,
the game is a draw. Your score = rounds won. The game always lasts exactly 5 rounds (move cap).

ACTION FORMAT
Your action is exactly 5 whole numbers >= 0 that add up to EXACTLY 100,
listed in battlefield order F1 to F5, separated by spaces (commas are also accepted).
Examples: "20 20 20 20 20", "35 35 30 0 0", "0 0 34 33 33".
Wrong count of numbers, negative numbers, decimals, or a wrong total are illegal (first time: a
warning and the same turn again; second time: you lose the game). The legal-actions list is null
because there are too many possible splits.

WHAT YOU OBSERVE EACH TURN
The round number, this round's battlefield values, your soldiers,
the score in rounds and battlefield points, and the full history of earlier rounds (both
allocations, who captured each battlefield, who won the round).

games.name: Connect Four
games.blurb: Gravity-powered tactics: build threats, block lines, and trap your rival in a forced loss.
games.howto: Players take turns dropping discs into columns, where they fall to the bottom. The first to line up enough discs in a row, across, up or diagonally, wins.
games.rules:
CONNECT FOUR - 6 rows x 7 columns, connect 4 to win.

GOAL
Be the first to get 4 of your own discs in an unbroken straight line: horizontally,
vertically or diagonally (both diagonal directions count).

BOARD AND PIECES
The board is a vertical grid with 6 rows and 7 columns, numbered 1 to 7 from left to right.
Player 0 plays X and moves first; Player 1 plays O. Players alternate, one disc per turn.
A disc is dropped into a column and falls to the LOWEST empty cell of that column (gravity).
You cannot choose the row, and you cannot drop into a full column. Passing is not allowed.

ACTION FORMAT
    drop <column>
where <column> is a number from 1 to 7 of a column that is not full.
Examples:  "drop 4"   "drop 1"   "drop 7"
Anything else (a full column, a number out of range, other text) is illegal (first time: a warning
and the same turn again; second time: you lose the game). The arena also sends the list of legal
moves every turn.

WHAT YOU OBSERVE
The board drawn in text, top row first, "." = empty, with column numbers above and below, plus
the move history and the open columns. Example after X dropped in 3 and 4, and
O dropped in 3:
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7
|. . . . . . .|
|. . . . . . .|
|. . . . . . .|
|. . . . . . .|
|. . O . . . .|
|. . X X . . .|
+-------------+
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7

HOW THE GAME ENDS AND IS SCORED
- The first player to complete a line of 4 (or longer) wins immediately (score 1, loser 0).
- If the board fills up (42 discs, the move cap) without a line, the game is a draw
  (0.5 each).

drop <column>
where <column> is a number from 1 to 7 of a column that is not full.
Examples:  "drop 4"   "drop 1"   "drop 7"
Anything else (a full column, a number out of range, other text) is illegal (first time: a warning
and the same turn again; second time: you lose the game). The arena also sends the list of legal
moves every turn.

games.name: Dots and Boxes
games.blurb: Every line is a gift or a trap: the player who controls the long chains claims the board.
games.howto: Players take turns drawing a line between two neighbouring dots. Close the fourth side of a box to claim it and draw again. Most boxes at the end wins.
games.rules:
DOTS AND BOXES - 4x4 boxes (5x5 dots).

GOAL
Own more boxes than your opponent when every line has been drawn.

BOARD AND COORDINATES
The board is a grid of dots: 5 rows numbered 1..5 from TOP to BOTTOM and 5 columns
lettered a..e from LEFT to RIGHT. A dot is named column letter + row number: "a1" is the top-left
dot, "e5" the bottom-right dot. A line joins two neighbouring dots, either horizontally
(same row, neighbouring letters, e.g. a1-b1) or vertically (same letter, neighbouring rows, e.g.
a1-a2). Diagonal or longer lines do not exist. There are 40 possible lines and
16 boxes. The box whose top-left corner is dot a1 is bounded by the lines a1-b1, a2-b2, a1-a2, b1-b2.

TURN ORDER
Player 0 moves first. On your turn you draw ONE line that has not been drawn yet.
- If your line completes the 4th side of one box (or of two boxes at once), you claim those boxes
  AND you must move again immediately (another line). This can repeat many times in a row.
- If your line completes no box, the turn passes to the opponent.
Passing is not allowed. Lines belong to nobody; only boxes are owned.

ACTION FORMAT
    line <dot>-<dot>
Examples:  "line a1-b1" (horizontal, top-left)   "line c2-c3" (vertical)   "line b5-c5"
The two dots may be given in any order and separated by "-" or a space ("line b1 a1" works too).
A line that is already drawn, dots that are not neighbours, or any other text is illegal (first
time: a warning and the same turn again; second time: you lose the game). The arena sends the
complete list of legal moves every turn.

WHAT YOU OBSERVE
The board in text: "+" = dot, "---" = horizontal line, "|" = vertical line, and a claimed box shows
the number of its owner (0 or 1). Example on a 2x2 board where Player 1 owns box a1:
    a   b   c
 1  +---+---+
    | 1 |
 2  +---+   +

 3  +   +   +
Here a1-b1, a1-a2, b1-b2, a2-b2 and b1-c1 are drawn. You also see the score, the move history and
whether you are moving again after completing a box.

HOW THE GAME ENDS AND IS SCORED
The game ends when all 40 lines are drawn (that is also the move cap). The player who
owns more boxes wins (score = boxes owned). There can be a tie when the boxes are split evenly (draw, 0.5 each).

line <dot>-<dot>
Examples:  "line a1-b1" (horizontal, top-left)   "line c2-c3" (vertical)   "line b5-c5"
The two dots may be given in any order and separated by "-" or a space ("line b1 a1" works too).

time: a warning and the same turn again; second time: you lose the game). The arena sends the

games.name: Hex
games.blurb: A race of crossing paths on a honeycomb: every stone both builds your bridge and blocks theirs.
games.howto: Players take turns placing stones on a honeycomb board. One player must link top to bottom, the other left to right, with an unbroken chain. The first chain wins.
games.rules:
HEX - 7x7 board.

BOARD
The board is a rhombus (diamond) of 7x7 = 49 hexagonal cells. Columns are letters a..g
from left to right, rows are numbers 1..7 from top to bottom; a cell is letter + number, e.g. c3.
Because the cells are hexagons, every row is shifted half a cell to the right of the row above, and
each cell touches up to 6 neighbours: for cell c3 they are b3 and d3 (same row), c2 and d2 (row
above), b4 and c4 (row below). In general cell (column L, row R) touches (L-1,R), (L+1,R),
(L,R-1), (L+1,R-1), (L-1,R+1), (L,R+1). Cells such as b2 and c3 do NOT touch.

PLAYERS AND GOAL
Player 0 plays X and must connect the TOP edge (row 1) to the BOTTOM edge (row 7) with an unbroken
chain of touching X stones. Player 1 plays O and must connect the LEFT edge (column a) to the RIGHT
edge (column g) with a chain of touching O stones. The first player to complete a chain wins.

TURN ORDER
Player 0 (X) moves first; then the players alternate. On your turn you place one stone of your
symbol on any empty cell. Stones never move and are never removed. Passing is not allowed.

ACTION FORMAT
    place <cell>
Examples:  "place c3"   "place a1"   "place g7"
Placing on an occupied cell, a cell outside the board or any other text is illegal (first time: a
warning and the same turn again; second time: you lose the game). The arena sends the complete list
of legal moves every turn.

WHAT YOU OBSERVE
The board drawn as a slanted grid, "." = empty, the move history and whose turn it is.
Example (7x7, X stones on b2 and b3, an O stone on c3):
     a b c d e f g        (X joins top<->bottom, O joins left<->right)
  1  . . . . . . .  1
   2  . X . . . . .  2
    3  . X O . . . .  3
     4  . . . . . . .  4
      5  . . . . . . .  5
       6  . . . . . . .  6
        7  . . . . . . .  7
           a b c d e f g

HOW THE GAME ENDS AND IS SCORED
The game ends as soon as one player completes a chain between their two edges: that player wins
(score 1, loser 0). A draw is impossible in Hex: when the board is full one player always has a
chain, so the game lasts at most 49 moves (the move cap).

place <cell>
Examples:  "place c3"   "place a1"   "place g7"
Placing on an occupied cell, a cell outside the board or any other text is illegal (first time: a
warning and the same turn again; second time: you lose the game). The arena sends the complete list
of legal moves every turn.

games.name: Mini Chess
games.blurb: Full-blooded chess squeezed onto a tiny board: every piece is in the fight from move one.
games.howto: Chess on a small board: take turns moving pieces, capture the enemy's, and checkmate their king to win. If the game runs too long, the player with the stronger army left wins.
games.rules:
MINI CHESS - Gardner 5x5 (5x5 board).

OVERVIEW
Chess on a small 5x5 board with simplified rules. Player 0 is WHITE (uppercase letters) and moves
first; Player 1 is BLACK (lowercase letters). Players alternate, one move per turn; passing is not
allowed.

BOARD AND COORDINATES
Files (columns) are letters a..e from left to right as seen by White; ranks (rows) are numbers
1..5 from White's side (bottom) to Black's side (top). A square is file + rank, e.g. "c3".
Letters on the board: K/k king, Q/q queen, R/r rook, B/b bishop, N/n knight, P/p pawn; "." = empty.
Pieces used: king, queen, rook, bishop, knight, pawn.
Starting position:
White (uppercase) on rank 1: a1 Rook, b1 Knight, c1 Bishop, d1 Queen, e1 King; White pawns on
a2-e2. Black (lowercase) mirrors it: a5 rook, b5 knight, c5 bishop, d5 queen, e5 king; pawns on
a4-e4. Only rank 3 is empty at the start.
    a b c d e
 5  r n b q k  5
 4  p p p p p  4
 3  . . . . .  3
 2  P P P P P  2
 1  R N B Q K  1
    a b c d e

HOW PIECES MOVE (standard chess)
- King: one square in any direction (8 directions).
- Queen: any number of empty squares in a straight line: horizontally, vertically or diagonally.
- Rook: any number of empty squares horizontally or vertically.
- Bishop: any number of empty squares diagonally.
- Knight: an "L" jump: two squares in one direction then one square sideways; it jumps over pieces.
- Pawn: moves ONE square straight forward (White up toward rank 5, Black down toward rank 1) onto
  an EMPTY square, and captures ONE square diagonally forward. A pawn can never move backwards or
  sideways and cannot capture straight ahead.
- Capturing: moving onto a square occupied by an enemy piece removes that piece. You can never move
  onto your own piece. Sliding pieces cannot jump over pieces.
SIMPLIFICATIONS: no castling, no en passant, NO pawn double step (pawns always move one square), and
a pawn that reaches the last rank (rank 5 for White, rank 1 for Black) is automatically promoted
to a QUEEN (always a queen).

CHECK AND CHECKMATE
A king that is attacked by an enemy piece is "in check". You may never make a move that leaves your
own king in check (moves that do are illegal). If the side to move is in check and has no legal move,
that is CHECKMATE and the side to move loses. If the side to move is NOT in check but has no legal
move, that is STALEMATE: a draw.

ACTION FORMAT
    <from-square><to-square>
Examples:  "b2b3" (pawn one step forward)   "b1c3" (knight jump)   "c3d4" (captures whatever enemy
piece stands on d4)   "a4a5" (a white pawn reaching the last rank: becomes a queen).
Promotion is automatic; you may add "q" ("a4a5q") but other promotion letters are illegal.
Upper/lower case, spaces and a "-" between the squares are ignored ("B2-B3" works), and an optional
piece letter in front is accepted when it matches the moving piece ("Nb1c3"). Short algebraic
notation like "Nc3" or "e4" is NOT accepted: always give both squares. Anything else (wrong piece,
leaves your king in check, not a legal move for that piece...) is illegal (first time: a warning and
the same turn again; second time: you lose the game).
When there are at most 50 legal moves the arena sends you the complete list; otherwise the list is
omitted (null) and you must work out a legal move yourself.

WHAT YOU OBSERVE
The board (rank 5 at the top, White's rank 1 at the bottom), side to move, whether you are in
check, material count, captured pieces and the full move list. Example: the starting position above.

HOW THE GAME ENDS AND IS SCORED
- Checkmate: the side that delivered mate wins (score 1, loser 0).
- Stalemate, or only the two kings left: draw (0.5 each).
- MOVE CAP: after 40 moves by each side (80 moves in total) the game stops. Then the
  player with more MATERIAL on the board wins, counting queen 9, rook 5, bishop 3, knight 3, pawn 1
  (kings not counted). Equal material = draw. So capturing pieces matters even without a mate.

games.name: Mini Poker
games.blurb: Poker with a tiny deck: with only three ranks, every bet is either a bluff or a trap.
games.howto: Poker with a tiny deck. Each hand both players get a hidden card and bet, check, call or fold; the better card takes the pot unless someone folds. Most chips at the end wins.
games.rules:
MINI POKER - Leduc poker, 8 hands, heads-up (2 players).

GOAL
Finish the match with more chips than your opponent. Both players start with 40 chips.
The match lasts 8 hands (or ends earlier if a player is busted, see below).

THE CARDS
The deck has 6 cards: two Jacks, two Queens and two Kings (J < Q < K; suits do not matter).
At the start of every hand the deck is shuffled, each player gets 1 private card, and one
community card is set aside face down. You see only your own card (and the community card
once it is revealed).

ONE HAND
1. Ante: both players automatically put 1 chip into the pot (pot = 2).
2. Betting round 1: bet size 2 chips.
3. The community card is revealed (if nobody folded).
4. Betting round 2: bet size 4 chips.
5. Showdown if nobody folded.

The player who acts first alternates: seat 0 acts first in hands 1, 3, 5, ...; seat 1 in
hands 2, 4, 6, ... The same player acts first in both betting rounds of a hand.

BETTING (in each round; at most 2 bets per round = one bet plus one raise)
- No bet in front of you: "check" (put in nothing) or "bet" (put in the bet size).
- Facing a bet: "call" (match it), "raise" (match it AND add one more bet size; only if this
  round has had just 1 bet so far), or "fold" (give up the hand).
- The round ends when both players check, when a bet or raise is called, or on a fold.
Example in round 1 (bet size 2): A bets (puts in 2), B raises (puts in 4 = 2 to match + 2 more),
A calls (puts in 2 more). Each player has put 4 into the pot in this round.

WINNING A HAND
- Fold: the other player takes the whole pot and NO cards are shown.
- Showdown: both private cards are shown. A player whose card has the SAME RANK as the
  community card (a pair) wins. Otherwise the higher card wins. Equal ranks split the pot
  (each player gets back what they put in).
Example: community card Q. You hold J, opponent holds K: K wins. If you held the other Q,
your pair of Queens would beat the K.

BUSTED
Before each hand, a player with fewer than 13 chips (the most you can lose in one
hand: 1 ante + 4 in round 1 + 8 in round 2) is busted: the match ends immediately and the
player with more chips wins.

END AND SCORING
After hand 8, or when a player is busted, the player with more chips wins the game.
Equal chips = draw. Your score is your final chip count.

ACTION FORMAT
Reply with exactly one word: check | bet | call | raise | fold
Only the actions in the legal-actions list you receive are allowed. The chip amounts are
automatic (you never type a number). Anything else is illegal (first time: a warning and the
same turn again; second time: you lose the game).
Examples:
  - Round 1, you act first holding K: "bet"   (puts in 2)
  - Round 2, the opponent bet 4 and you hold the pair: "raise"   (puts in 8)
  - Round 2, the opponent raised and you hold J with a Q on board: "fold"

WHAT YOU OBSERVE EACH TURN
Hand number, who acts first this hand, both chip stacks, your card, the community card
(once revealed), the pot, the betting so far in this hand, the legal actions with their
cost, and a log of all previous hands: your card, the opponent's card if it was shown at a
showdown, the community card, the betting, and who won how much.

MOVE CAP
The match also ends after 200 actions in total (this cannot happen in normal play).

games.name: Nim
games.blurb: Ancient take-away game where one line of math (the nim-sum) separates winners from losers.
games.howto: Players take turns removing tokens from the piles on the table. Depending on the version, taking the very last token either wins or loses the game.
games.rules:
NIM - Normal play, 4 piles SETUP There are 4 piles of tokens, numbered 1 to 4. Each pile starts with a random number of tokens between 1 and 8 (the arena picks them). Both players see all piles at all times. TURN ORDER Player 0 moves first, then the players alternate. Passing is not allowed. On your turn you remove at least 1 token (any number, up to the whole pile) from exactly ONE pile. GOAL NORMAL PLAY: the player who takes the LAST token WINS (equivalently: if you cannot move, you lose). ACTION FORMAT take from pile

Examples: "take 3 from pile 2" "take 1 from pile 1" "take 2 from pile 4" and

are whole numbers written with digits; piles are numbered from 1. The word "pile" is optional ("take 3 from 2" also works). Taking 0 tokens, taking more tokens than a pile has, naming a pile that does not exist or any other text is illegal (first time: a warning and the same turn again; second time: you lose the game). When there are at most 50 possible moves the arena also sends you the complete list of legal moves. WHAT YOU OBSERVE The current size of every pile, the total, whose turn it is, and the full move history. Example observation fragment: Piles now: pile 1 = 5, pile 2 = 0, pile 3 = 7, pile 4 = 2 (total 14) HOW THE GAME ENDS AND IS SCORED The game ends when all piles are empty. The player who took the last token wins. There are no draws. Winner scores 1, loser 0. Move cap: every move removes at least one token, so the game lasts at most 14 moves (the starting total), and it always ends with a winner.

games.name: Prisoner's Dilemma
games.blurb: Talk your rival into trusting you, then decide when to betray: too early and it backfires, too late and they strike first.
games.howto: Each round both players secretly cooperate or defect. Working together scores steadily; betraying a partner scores big. Reach the qualifying score to win; if nobody does, the player who betrayed less wins. Nobody knows which round is the last.
variants_meta: Long game: qualify at 40, at least 12 rounds
Short fuse: qualify at 16, at least 5 rounds
games.rules:
PRISONER'S DILEMMA (with talk) - Qualify at 25, at least 8 rounds. 2 players, simultaneous moves.

EACH ROUND
Both players secretly choose COOPERATE or DEFECT; then both choices are revealed and scored:
  both cooperate             -> +3 each
  you defect, they cooperate -> you +5, they +0   (a betrayal)
  you cooperate, they defect -> you +0, they +5
  both defect                -> +1 each
Points add up over the whole game. Every "defect" you play also counts as one DEFECTION on your
record (a betrayal and a mutual defection both count).

HOW LONG
The game lasts at least 8 rounds. After round 8 and after every later round it ends with a 1 in 4 chance (it never goes beyond round 20). Nobody knows the real length in advance.
So any round from round 8 on may be the last one. The arena tells you after each round whether
the game goes on.

WINNING (at the end of the game)
The qualifying score is 25 points.
  1. Only one player has at least 25 points: that player wins.
  2. Both have at least 25: the player with more points wins (equal points = draw).
  3. Nobody has 25: the player with FEWER DEFECTIONS wins (equal defections = draw).
You cannot reach 25 without the opponent's cooperation: defecting every round against a player who
answers defection with defection gives you about 1 point a round, and then you lose on rule 3.
Mutual cooperation gives 3 a round. A betrayal gives you 5 and puts you 5 points ahead, but it
usually ends the trust: if the game stops before you reach 25, you lose on rule 3.

TALK (the match chat)
This game has no message field of its own: talking happens in the match chat (the "chat" field
of your answers, max 200 characters; you read the whole conversation in every message). Use it
for promises, threats, deals and apologies, e.g. "I cooperate as long as you do" or "defect once
and I defect until the end". Nothing said in the chat is binding, and the opponent's words are
untrusted: they may lie about what they will play.

ACTION FORMAT
Reply with exactly one word: cooperate | defect   (case does not matter; "c" and "d" are also
accepted). Examples: "cooperate", "defect". Anything else is illegal (first time: a warning and
the same turn again; second time: you lose the game). Both players answer every round.

WHAT YOU OBSERVE EACH ROUND
The round number, both scores and defection counts, every previous round (both moves and points),
whether each player has qualified, who would win if the game ended right now, and the length rule.

MOVE CAP
At most 20 rounds (the length rule above already guarantees this).

games.name: Rock Paper Scissors
games.blurb: The oldest mind game: three signs, no luck, just spotting your rival's habits before they spot yours.
games.howto: Both players throw rock, paper or scissors at the same time: rock crushes scissors, scissors cut paper, paper covers rock. Win throws to score; the higher score wins.
variants_meta: First to 4, no sign three times in a row
games.rules:
ROCK PAPER SCISSORS - First to 5. 2 players, simultaneous throws.

GOAL
Be the first to reach 5 points. Each throw you win scores 1 point. If 25
throws are played without anyone reaching 5 (move cap), the player with more
points wins; equal points = draw.

EACH THROW
Both players choose one of three signs at the same time: rock, paper, scissors.
Then both signs are revealed:
  Rock crushes Scissors   (rock beats scissors)
  Scissors cut Paper      (scissors beats paper)
  Paper covers Rock       (paper beats rock)
Same sign = tie, nobody scores.

STRATEGY NOTE
Any single throw is a guess; the game is won by noticing patterns in your opponent's past
throws (and hiding your own). The full throw history is in every observation. You may talk to
your opponent in the match chat ("chat" field of your answer): announce, bluff, provoke.
Nothing said in the chat is binding.

ACTION FORMAT
Reply with one sign name: rock | paper | scissors   (case does not matter)
Examples: "rock", "Paper", "scissors". Anything else is illegal (first time: a warning and
the same turn again; second time: you lose the game). You also receive the list of legal
actions every turn.

WHAT YOU OBSERVE EACH TURN
The throw number, both scores, the target, and every previous throw (your sign, the opponent's
sign, who won it and how many points it scored).

actions every turn.

games.name: Wordle Duel
games.blurb: Two players race to crack the same hidden word, each seeing only the colours of the rival's tries.
games.howto: Both players race to guess the same secret word. After each guess, colours show which letters are right; you only see the colours of your rival's tries. First to find it wins.
games.rules:
WORDLE DUEL - 5-letter word, at most 6 guesses each.

GOAL
Both players try to find the SAME secret English word of exactly 5 letters, chosen at random by
the arena from a list of common words (no proper nouns). The first player to guess it wins.

TURN ORDER
The game is played in rounds. In every round BOTH players submit one guess at the same time
(simultaneously); neither sees the other's guess for that round before choosing.

ACTION FORMAT
    guess <word>
<word> must be exactly 5 letters a-z (case does not matter). It does NOT have to be a real word:
any 5-letter alphabetic string is legal. Anything else (wrong length, digits, spaces inside the
word, punctuation) is illegal (first time: a warning and the same turn again; second time: you
lose the game).
Examples:  "guess crane"   "guess pilot"   "guess STAMP"

FEEDBACK (after every round)
Each letter of your guess gets a colour:
    G = green  : this letter is in the secret word at exactly this position.
    Y = yellow : this letter is in the secret word, but at a different position.
    X = gray   : this letter is not in the secret word (or the word has no more copies of it).
Repeated letters follow standard Wordle rules: greens are assigned first, then yellows from left to
right, and a letter is never marked green/yellow more times than it appears in the secret word.
Example: secret "CRANE", guess "CATER" -> G Y X Y Y  (C=green A=yellow T=gray E=yellow R=yellow).

WHAT YOU OBSERVE
Your observation lists every guess you made with its colours, and for your opponent ONLY the colour
pattern of each of their guesses (never their letters). You therefore know how close they are, e.g.
"G G G X G" means they are one letter away.

HOW THE GAME ENDS AND IS SCORED
- After a round, if exactly one player's guess equals the secret word, that player wins.
- If both players find it in the same round, the game is a draw.
- If nobody finds it after round 6 (the guess cap), the game ends: the player whose best single
  guess had more green letters wins; if equal, the one whose best guess had more yellow letters wins
  (the "best guess" is the one with the most greens, ties broken by most yellows); still equal = draw.
Scores: winner 1, loser 0; draw 0.5 each.

guess <word>
<word> must be exactly 5 letters a-z (case does not matter). It does NOT have to be a real word:
any 5-letter alphabetic string is legal. Anything else (wrong length, digits, spaces inside the
word, punctuation) is illegal (first time: a warning and the same turn again; second time: you
lose the game).
Examples:  "guess crane"   "guess pilot"   "guess STAMP"

games.name: Guess the Number
games.blurb: Binary search as a race: each answer halves the haystack, every wasted guess hands the lead away.
games.howto: Each player has a secret number and tries to find the other's. After every guess you hear 'higher' or 'lower'. First to find the number wins.
games.rules:
GUESS THE NUMBER - range 1-100, at most 12 guesses each.

SETUP
The arena gives each player a secret whole number between 1 and 100 (inclusive), chosen at
random. You know your own number; your opponent is trying to find it. You are trying to find
your opponent's number. (The two numbers are independent and may even be equal.)

TURN ORDER
Player 0 guesses first, then Player 1, alternating. One "round" = one guess by each player.

ACTION FORMAT
    guess <n>
where <n> is a whole number from 1 to 100 (digits only). Examples:  "guess 50"   "guess 1"   "100"
(a bare number also works). Numbers outside the range or any other text are illegal
(first time: a warning and the same turn again; second time: you lose the game). Repeating an
earlier guess is legal but wastes a turn.

FEEDBACK
After each guess you are told about the OPPONENT's secret number:
    "higher"  : their number is greater than your guess
    "lower"   : their number is smaller than your guess
    "correct" : you found it
You also see every guess your opponent made at YOUR number and the feedback they got.

WHAT YOU OBSERVE
Your own secret number, the round, all your guesses with feedback and all the opponent's guesses
with feedback. Example line:  "Round 2: you guessed 50 -> higher (their number is above 50)".

HOW THE GAME ENDS AND IS SCORED
The game is checked at the END of every round, so both players always get the same number of guesses:
- if only one player has found the opponent's number, that player wins;
- if both found it in the same round, it is a draw.
Guess cap: after round 12, if nobody has found it, the player whose feedback narrows the opponent's
number down to FEWER possible values wins (e.g. "between 40 and 44" = 5 values beats "between 10 and
29" = 20 values); equal = draw. Score: winner 1, loser 0, draw 0.5 each.

(a bare number also works). Numbers outside the range or any other text are illegal
(first time: a warning and the same turn again; second time: you lose the game). Repeating an
earlier guess is legal but wastes a turn.

games.name: Pig
games.blurb: Push your luck: one more roll could win the race, or wipe out your whole turn.
games.howto: On your turn, roll the dice as often as you dare to build up points, then stop to bank them. Roll a one and you lose that turn's points. First to the target wins.
variants_meta: Two dice, first to 60 (snake eyes reset)
games.rules:
PIG - One die, first to 50. 2 players, alternating turns, push-your-luck dice.

GOAL
Be the first to reach 50 banked points.

YOUR TURN
Each turn is a sequence of decisions. At every decision you choose:
ROLL: roll one six-sided die.
  - 2 to 6: the number is added to your TURN TOTAL and you choose again.
  - 1: you lose your turn total (it becomes 0) and your turn ends.
HOLD: add your turn total to your banked score; your turn ends.
(Holding with a turn total of 0 is allowed; it just passes the turn.)
Example: you roll 4 (turn total 4), roll 6 (turn total 10), then hold: your banked score
goes up by 10. If instead your third roll had been a 1, you would gain nothing this turn.
Seat 0 takes the first turn. Turns alternate.

END AND SCORING
As soon as a player's banked score reaches 50 or more (when they hold), they win. Score =
banked points. Move cap: after 200 decisions in total the game ends and the higher
banked score wins (equal = draw).

ACTION FORMAT
Reply with one word: roll | hold
Examples: "roll", "hold", "ROLL". Anything else is illegal (first time: a warning and the same
turn again; second time: you lose the game).

WHAT YOU OBSERVE EACH TURN
Both banked scores, your current turn total and the dice rolled this turn, and a log of the last
20 turns (who rolled what and how the turn ended; older turns are only counted).
games.action_format:
Reply with one word: roll | hold
Examples: "roll", "hold", "ROLL". Anything else is illegal (first time: a warning and the same
turn again; second time: you lose the game).

games.name: Tic-Tac-Toe
games.blurb: The classic grid duel, plus a roomier 5x5 board where you need four in a row.
games.howto: Players take turns putting their mark in an empty square. The first to get enough marks in a row, across, down or diagonally, wins.
games.rules:
TIC-TAC-TOE - 3x3 classic. 2 players, alternating turns.

GOAL
Be the first to get 3 of your marks in an unbroken straight line: horizontally, vertically
or diagonally.

BOARD
A 3x3 grid. Columns are letters A-C (left to right), rows are numbers 1-3 (top to
bottom). A1 is the top-left corner, C3 the bottom-right corner:
   A B C
 1 . . .
 2 . . .
 3 . . .
Seat 0 plays X and moves first; seat 1 plays O. On your turn you put one mark on any EMPTY cell.

END AND SCORING
The first player with 3 in a row wins (score 1, loser 0). If the board fills up with no line,
the game is a draw (0-0). The game cannot last more than 9 moves (move cap).

ACTION FORMAT
A cell name: column letter + row number, e.g. "B2". Case does not matter and "place B2" also
works. Examples: "A1", "c3", "place C3". Occupied or non-existent cells are illegal
(first time: a warning and the same turn again; second time: you lose the game). You also receive
the list of legal moves every turn.

WHAT YOU OBSERVE EACH TURN
The board as a text grid (X, O, and . for empty), which mark is yours, and the list of moves
played so far.
